overview.text: Deng Xiaoping was China’s most powerful leader during the 1989 Tiananmen protests, although he did not hold the presidency. After emerging as the central figure in the late 1970s, he promoted economic reforms and greater contact with the outside world. In spring 1989, students and other citizens gathered in Beijing to demand political change. Senior Communist Party figures disagreed over how to respond. Declassified accounts identify Deng and other party elders as decisive supporters of martial law and the military action that ended the demonstrations in early June. Troops killed protesters and bystanders, prompting international condemnation and a sharp disruption in China’s relations with the United States.

key_facts.text: Deng became the dominant Chinese leader after the late 1970s without being president.
His reforms opened parts of China’s economy to market forces and foreign exchange.
The Tiananmen protests began in Beijing in spring 1989.
Party elders led by Deng called on the army to restore order after leaders deadlocked over martial law.
Chinese troops used deadly force against protesters and bystanders in early June 1989.

overview.text: Jacob Zuma is a South African politician who served as president from 2009 until his resignation in 2018. He had previously taken part in the anti-apartheid movement, held senior positions in the African National Congress, and served as the country’s deputy president. After he left office, a judicial commission investigating allegations of state capture ordered him to testify. Zuma failed to comply with a Constitutional Court order to appear and provide evidence. In 2021, the court found him in contempt and imposed a fifteen-month prison sentence. His imprisonment concerned disobedience of a court order, not a finding that the commission’s corruption allegations had been proved.

key_facts.text: Zuma became South Africa’s president in May 2009.
He resigned as president in February 2018.
Before the presidency, he served as South Africa’s deputy president and led the ANC.

The court imposed a fifteen-month prison sentence in June 2021.

overview.text: Koxinga, also called Zheng Chenggong, was a seventeenth-century military leader loyal to the fallen Ming dynasty. During the Ming-Qing transition, he crossed to Taiwan with his forces. In 1661 his forces attacked Dutch East India Company positions near present-day Tainan, including Fort Zeelandia. The Dutch surrendered in 1662, ending their colonial rule in southwestern Taiwan. Koxinga established a Ming-loyalist government there, commonly called the Kingdom of Tungning. His descendants continued to rule until Qing forces defeated the Zheng regime in 1683, making his campaign a turning point in Taiwan’s political history.

He was a Ming loyalist resisting the Qing takeover of China.
His troops landed in Taiwan and attacked Dutch positions in 1661.

overview.text: The Kingdom of Greece was the monarchical form of the modern Greek state that emerged after the war for independence from the Ottoman Empire. Otto became its first king in 1832 and initially ruled as an absolute monarch. An uprising in 1843 compelled a constitution, creating a constitutional monarchy. Otto was removed in 1862; George I then became king under a new constitutional arrangement that emphasized popular sovereignty. The monarchy was interrupted by a republic in the interwar period and later returned. After the military dictatorship ended, a referendum in December 1974 rejected restoration of the crown, and Greece adopted a republican constitutional order.

An uprising in 1843 led to the Constitution of 1844.
Otto was ousted in 1862 and George I succeeded him.
The Constitution of 1864 treated the people as the source of state power.

overview.text: Sutton Hoo is an early medieval burial ground in Suffolk, England, celebrated for an Anglo-Saxon ship burial. In 1939, excavators found the outline of a buried ship and a chamber containing weapons, metalwork, and an elaborate helmet. The objects point to a powerful person with links extending beyond East Anglia, but the individual’s identity remains unknown; King Rædwald is a leading suggestion. Coins help date the burial to around 625 CE. Acidic soil destroyed most organic remains, while chemical evidence showed that a body had once lain in the chamber. The discovery greatly expanded knowledge of wealth, craftsmanship, and long-distance connections in early Anglo-Saxon England.

key_facts.text: Sutton Hoo is a burial ground in Suffolk, England.
The major ship burial was uncovered in 1939.
The burial chamber held a helmet, sword, and other valuable objects.
Coins place the burial around 625 CE.
King Rædwald is a proposed occupant, but the buried person cannot be identified with certainty.

overview.text: The Russian Empire was the state ruled by Russia’s emperors from Peter the Great’s adoption of the imperial title in 1721 until the monarchy collapsed in 1917. Its territory stretched across northern Eurasia and included many peoples and languages. Peter’s victory over Sweden gave Russia a Baltic foothold, and Saint Petersburg became the imperial capital. During the nineteenth century, the state expanded in the Caucasus and Central Asia, while Alexander II emancipated the serfs in 1861. The last emperor, Nicholas II, abdicated during the February Revolution in March 1917. A provisional government took power before the Bolsheviks seized power later that year.

overview.text: Jan Hus was a Czech preacher and reformer active in Prague in the early fifteenth century. At Bethlehem Chapel he preached in Czech and called for changes in church conduct, including criticism of clerical wealth and abuses. He wrote religious works in both Czech and Latin and became entangled in disputes over church authority and teachings associated with John Wycliffe. After church authorities excommunicated him, Hus traveled to the Council of Constance to defend his views. The council condemned him, and he was burned at the stake in 1415. His death helped energize the Hussite reform movement in Bohemia.

He wrote religious works in Czech and Latin.

overview.text: A phalanx was a close-packed infantry formation used by ancient Greek armies. The best-known Greek version consisted of hoplites, heavily equipped foot soldiers who carried long spears and large shields. They advanced in ranks so that neighboring shields overlapped, giving the front line collective protection. Its effectiveness depended on discipline and on keeping the formation intact; a broken line exposed soldiers to attack. Greek city-states relied on this style of fighting for centuries. Philip II of Macedon later adapted the formation with a smaller shield and a much longer spear called the sarissa, creating a different Macedonian phalanx used by his successors.

key_facts.text: A Greek hoplite was an armored foot soldier with a spear and shield.
Hoplite phalanxes advanced with overlapping shields.
Some phalanxes were eight or more ranks deep.
Keeping ranks together was essential to the formation’s protection.
Philip II of Macedon introduced a longer spear called the sarissa into his version.

overview.text: The Stasi was the common name for East Germany’s Ministry for State Security, founded in 1950. It served the ruling Socialist Unity Party as a secret police force and foreign intelligence agency. Its officers watched suspected opponents, intercepted communications, carried out interrogations, and operated detention centers. A large network of unofficial collaborators supplied information from workplaces, schools, and personal relationships. In the 1970s, the ministry increasingly used covert intimidation and reputation attacks alongside surveillance. Despite this reach, it did not eliminate public opposition. After East Germany’s peaceful revolution, surviving Stasi files became an important record of how the dictatorship monitored citizens.

key_facts.text: The Ministry for State Security was founded in East Germany in 1950.
Stasi was a common name for the ministry.
It functioned as domestic secret police and a foreign intelligence agency.
Unofficial collaborators reported on colleagues, friends, and opposition groups.
The Stasi used phone bugging, observation, arrests, and interrogations.

overview.text: The Babylonian Captivity refers to the forced exile of people from the kingdom of Judah to Babylonia in the sixth century BCE. After Nebuchadnezzar II captured Jerusalem in 597 BCE, King Jehoiachin and members of the royal court were taken away. A later revolt brought another Babylonian siege, the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, and further deportations. Judean communities continued to live and work in Babylonia, as surviving cuneiform records attest. When the Persian ruler Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, exiles were allowed to return. Biblical accounts describe the return and rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple, while Babylonian records independently attest the earlier conquest.

King Jehoiachin and elite Judeans were deported to Babylonia.
A second siege destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 586 BCE.
Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE.
Under Persian rule, Judean exiles could return to Jerusalem.
